opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because the whole power of AlphaEvolve comes from the evaluation loop. The system proposes a candidate, maybe a program, an algorithm, or a construction in mathematics, and then something has to tell it how good that candidate is. Where that "something" is a machine-checkable function, like the running time of a kernel, the number of multiplications in a matrix multiplication scheme, or whether a construction satisfies some bound, you can run that loop thousands or millions of times. That scale is what lets the evolutionary search really explore the space.

When you put a human in that loop, the first constraint is simply throughput. Humans are slow and expensive compared to a computer evaluating a function. If each candidate needs a person to look at it and say "this is better" or "this is worse," you can't do millions of iterations. You might get hundreds, or a few thousand if you're lucky. So the search has to be much more sample-efficient, and you need to be much more careful about which candidates you actually show to people.

The second constraint is consistency and noise. A well-defined evaluator gives you the same answer every time. Humans don't. Different people have different preferences, the same person might judge differently on Monday than on Friday, and they get fatigued. An evolutionary process is very good at exploiting whatever signal you give it, and if that signal is noisy or inconsistent, it can chase the noise rather than real improvement.

Related to that is the problem of exploitation, or what people sometimes call reward hacking. Any optimizer that's powerful enough will find the gaps in your evaluator. With code evaluators, we've learned to be quite careful about that, making sure the program is actually correct and not just gaming the metric. With humans, the gaps are subtler. The system might learn to produce things that look impressive or persuasive to a human rater without actually being better on the dimension you care about. That's a real risk, and it's harder to detect.

And then there's the question of what humans can actually judge. For a lot of the problems where AlphaEvolve shines, the quality of a solution isn't something a person can eyeball. You can't look at an algorithm and know how fast it runs at scale, or look at a mathematical construction and immediately see whether it improves a bound. Humans are great at judging some things, like aesthetics, readability, whether something makes sense in context, but those aren't always the things you're optimizing.

So I think the sweet spot is probably hybrid. You use automated evaluators for the bulk of the search, where they're reliable and cheap, and you bring humans in at key points: to define what "good" means, to check the most promising candidates, to steer the search when it's going in a strange direction, or to judge qualities that are genuinely hard to formalize. You can also try to learn a model of human judgment from a smaller number of human evaluations and use that as a proxy, although then you inherit all the usual concerns about whether the proxy faithfully captures what people actually want.

In a way, that's the deeper point. A lot of the work in making these systems useful is really the work of articulating what you want precisely enough that it can be evaluated. Where we can do that, the system can do amazing things. Where we can't, the human becomes the bottleneck, and the challenge is designing the loop so that human time is used where it adds the most value.

r001.rationale: The response says human evaluation is slow and expensive, limiting the loop to hundreds or perhaps a few thousand evaluations instead of millions.

r002.rationale: It says people cannot reliably judge a program’s performance by inspection, such as knowing how fast an algorithm runs at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a really good question, and I think it gets at the heart of what makes AlphaEvolve work and also where its boundaries are.

The whole premise of AlphaEvolve is that you have an evolutionary loop. The language model proposes candidate programs, you evaluate them, you keep the ones that score well, and you iterate. And the thing that makes that loop go fast is that the evaluator is automatic. You can run it thousands or millions of times. For a matrix multiplication algorithm, you can verify correctness and count the operations. For a data center scheduling heuristic, you can simulate it. The evaluator is cheap, it's deterministic, and crucially, it doesn't get tired.

Now, when you put a human in that position, you lose almost all of those properties. The first constraint is just throughput. A human can look at maybe tens of candidates in a day, not millions. So the search is starved. You're essentially doing a very expensive, very slow form of hill climbing.

The second constraint is consistency. If I show you two programs and ask which is better, and then I show you the same two programs tomorrow, you might give me a different answer. That noise is poison for an evolutionary process, because the selection pressure is what drives the whole thing. If the signal is noisy, you're mostly selecting on noise.

The third one, which I think is the most subtle, is that humans are not very good at evaluating things that are genuinely novel. If AlphaEvolve finds a construction that no one has seen before, the human evaluator has to actually understand it to judge it. And in the cases that matter most, that understanding might take a mathematician weeks. So the human is slowest precisely where the system is most interesting.

And then there's the exploitation problem. Any optimizer will find the cracks in its reward signal. With a human, those cracks are things like plausibility, length, confident-sounding explanations. So you end up optimizing for what looks good to a person rather than what is good.

So what we've generally tried to do is push humans up a level. Instead of being the evaluator, the human designs the evaluator. They encode what they care about into something that can run automatically, even if it's only a proxy. And then the human's judgment comes in at the end, looking at the small number of things that survived, and at the beginning, deciding what problem is worth attacking. That's where human taste is really valuable, and it's not where the bottleneck is.

r001.rationale: It says a human can assess only tens of candidates a day, compared with the thousands or millions needed for the search, limiting throughput.

r002.rationale: It explains that humans may struggle to understand and judge genuinely novel programs, sometimes needing weeks to assess them.

astra-6.text:
I think the main constraint is the speed and scale of evaluation. If you have a human judging every candidate that AlphaEvolve produces, that becomes a bottleneck. And people’s judgments can vary, so you also have to think about how consistent the feedback is.

There’s also a distinction between being able to judge an answer and being able to specify what you want. A human might look at a solution and say, “That’s a good solution,” but it can be much harder to turn that judgment into a reliable evaluation procedure.

So I think a useful role for humans is to help define the objective and develop the evaluator, and then inspect the results. Where you can automate evaluation, you can run a much larger search. Where you really need human judgment for every step, the approach becomes more constrained.

r001.rationale: It says human evaluation of every candidate would become a speed and scale bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It notes that judgments can vary and that turning a human judgment of a solution into a reliable evaluation procedure is difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
The main constraint is the number of evaluations you need. AlphaEvolve can generate and test a large number of candidate programs, and if a human has to look at every candidate, that quickly becomes a bottleneck. There’s also the question of consistency: different people may judge the same result differently, and even one person’s judgments can change over time.

So humans can help define what we care about and assess whether the results are useful, but the inner loop really benefits from an automated evaluator—something that can give reliable feedback quickly. If you can’t turn your objective into a test like that, applying AlphaEvolve becomes much harder.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve generates many candidates and having a human inspect every one quickly becomes a bottleneck, identifying evaluation volume as a scaling constraint.

r002.rationale: It mentions inconsistent judgments and assessing whether results are useful, but does not clearly identify humans’ ability to accurately assess the program’s intended property as a constraint.
